q1: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY ID,VIEW_DATE HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY ID,VIEW_DATE HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
counterexample: INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (1, 101, 201, '2023-01-01'); INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (2, 102, 201, '2023-01-01'); INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (3, 103, 201, '2023-01-02');
explanation: Q1 groups by VIEW_DATE and VIEWER_ID, while Q2 groups by ID (which is an alias for VIEWER_ID) and VIEW_DATE. This difference in grouping affects the results, especially when there are multiple view dates for the same viewer.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have at least two view dates for the same viewer, and the viewer should have viewed at least two different articles on one of those dates.
